title: The Iran War Has Put Venezuela’s Oil Back in the Spotlight | OilPrice.com
text:
Iran Says It's Found Ways to Dodge U.S. Oil Blockade

The U.S. restarted major strikes on Iran this week, hitting missile, radar, and other military installations along the southern coast and on Larak Island. Iran retaliated against U.S. positions across the Gulf and Jordan, and also continued attacking commercial shipping, with two supertankers carrying Saudi crude struck near Hormuz and two sailors killed aboard a Saudi-owned vessel. The civilian toll from the renewed U.S. campaign is drawing scrutiny after a strike hit a wedding in southern Iran, killing five people and injuring dozens, which Vance says is now being investigated. The shipping losses are piling up as well, with more than 70 attacks recorded since the war began and maritime insurers now facing roughly $2 billion in war-risk claims. Hormuz premiums have risen to as much as 40-60X prewar levels, with Lloyd’s List estimating insurance alone is adding roughly $7-$8 to the cost of a barrel. There is no diplomatic track to offset the military escalation for now: Vance said Thursday the U.S. will not negotiate while Iran continues attacking commercial shipping.

Chevron is putting more than $7 billion into Venezuela over the next five years in a major bet that Trump’s overhaul of the country’s oil sector will hold. The company plans to more than double its Venezuelan production to around 600,000 bpd. At the same time, U.S.-backed NABEP (North American Blue Energy Partners) has secured majority control of a company holding 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields containing around 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, with nearly $100 billion of investment planned. Several of those fields were previously operated by Chinese and Russian companies, prompting Beijing this week to demand protection for Chinese companies’ existing rights. China spent years lending billions to Caracas and securing access to Venezuelan crude while U.S. investment was largely frozen out. Eni also signed expansion agreements this week, although Exxon and ConocoPhillips have yet to make comparable commitments.

Israel’s far-right officials are publicly pushing Trump to help facilitate the ethnic cleansing of Gaza by using U.S. money and diplomatic leverage to find countries willing to take Palestinians driven from the territory. Defense Minister Israel Katz said Wednesday that there is ultimately “no real solution for Gaza” without migration and claimed countries willing to receive Palestinians are waiting for U.S. backing before proceeding. That backing would mean considerably more than Washington simply approving the plan. Israel wants the U.S. to help persuade prospective host governments to participate, potentially using financial incentives, diplomatic pressure and other inducements that Israel cannot offer on its own.

Headlines heralding Libya’s latest election deal are getting well ahead of the reality. The country’s rival factions have agreed on another path toward national elections, this time within two years, but the agreement leaves Libya with competing governments and offers no clear mechanism for creating the unified executive required before those elections can take place.

Chevron and Shell are lining up for a new deepwater position in Ghana, signing a preliminary agreement for production rights over the South Deepwater Tano Cape Three Points block. No investment figures have been disclosed. Ghana’s production has fallen sharply over the past 6-7 years because its onshore fields are maturing. The Chevron-Shell agreement is still early stage.

Azerbaijan is buying directly into the U.S. gas supply feeding the Gulf Coast LNG boom. State-owned SOCAR has agreed to pay Comstock Resources $1.65 billion in cash for stakes across its Haynesville shale and midstream business, including 20% of its Legacy Haynesville assets, 15% of Western Haynesville and 15% of Pinnacle Gas Services. Comstock keeps operatorship. SOCAR has spent years building its position as a gas producer and exporter around the Caspian and Europe; the deal gives it its first major upstream position in the U.S.

Shell is buying into two BP-operated offshore prospects, agreeing to take 30% of BP’s Conifer prospect in the Gulf of Mexico and 50% of the Tupinamba block in Brazil’s Santos Basin, with BP retaining operatorship of both. No purchase price was disclosed. The Brazilian acreage is the more interesting of the two after BP’s nearby Bumerangue discovery gave the company its largest discovery in 25 years, with BP estimating around 8 billion barrels of liquids in place. Shell already has a major Brazilian deepwater business, while the Gulf of Mexico is one of its most profitable producing regions.
